flashcards.q: What are the typical lifetimes and roles of access tokens vs refresh tokens?
flashcards.a: Access token: JWT, 5-15 min TTL, stateless verification, used on every API request. Refresh token: opaque, DB-tracked, days-to-weeks TTL, used ONLY to mint new access tokens.

flashcards.q: What does refresh token rotation mean, and why is rotation alone insufficient security?
flashcards.a: Every refresh invalidates the presented token and issues a new one. Rotation alone is just hygiene -- if an attacker has a copy and uses it before the legit client, they get the next valid token in the chain; nothing detects that theft happened.

flashcards.q: What is reuse detection and what's the correct response when it triggers?
flashcards.a: Presenting an already-rotated (invalidated) refresh token is proof a copy exists somewhere illegitimate. Correct response: revoke the ENTIRE token family (not just the flagged token), force re-login, and alert -- because you can't know which token in the chain the attacker currently holds.

flashcards.q: What race condition does rotation introduce, and how is it handled in production?
flashcards.a: A legitimate client retry (network timeout, double-fire) can present the same still-valid token twice, indistinguishable from theft. Production systems add a short grace window (a few seconds) that returns the SAME already-issued reissued pair for a same-token retry, rather than flagging it as reuse.

flashcards.q: What is the worst-case exposure window after a security team revokes a compromised account's access, in the access/refresh hybrid?
flashcards.a: Exactly the access-token's TTL -- revoking the refresh token stops new access tokens from being minted, but any already-issued access token keeps working until its own exp regardless of the revocation action.

flashcards.q: What is TTL caching in the token-lifecycle sense (distinct from JWKS caching), and what's the 'stacked staleness' risk?
flashcards.a: Authorization servers often cache the underlying permission lookup for the duration of the access-token TTL rather than re-querying on every mint. Stacking a cached-permission TTL with a long access-token TTL can compound into a much longer effective staleness window than either alone.

flashcards.q: Compare localStorage vs httpOnly cookie for storing browser-based tokens.
flashcards.a: localStorage: fully JS-readable, full XSS exfiltration risk, zero CSRF risk -- OWASP advises against it for sensitive tokens. httpOnly cookie: JS cannot read the raw value (blocks exfiltration) but reopens CSRF (mitigate with SameSite + anti-CSRF token) -- the mainstream 2026 default for sensitive browser tokens.

flashcards.q: Does an httpOnly cookie fully solve the XSS problem?
flashcards.a: No -- it prevents exfiltration of the raw token value, but a live XSS payload can still ride the httpOnly cookie to make authenticated requests AS the user while it's executing. It limits blast radius but doesn't replace closing the XSS vulnerability itself.

flashcards.q: What does DPoP (RFC 9449) add beyond reuse detection?
flashcards.a: Reuse detection is DETECTIVE -- it catches theft only after a race between the legit client and attacker, and whichever loses gets flagged (possibly the legit user). DPoP is PREVENTIVE -- it cryptographically binds the token to a client-held key via a signed per-request proof, so a stolen token without the key simply can't be used at all.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't the browser storage debate (localStorage vs cookies) apply to native mobile apps?
flashcards.a: Native apps store refresh tokens in OS-provided secure storage (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore) with no XSS-equivalent JS-injection vector. Threat model shifts to device compromise, malicious accessibility-service abuse, or jailbreak/root access instead.
